Apple Can be an Expensive AI Safe Haven
 
Plus, anticipating a substantial bear market and using AI for divorce advice
 
 
HECTOR RETAMAL/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

China has told the country’s biggest securities firms and banks to throttle back their work on initial public offerings and focus on boosting the struggling stock market, according to people familiar with the matter.

 

The China Securities Regulatory Commission said Monday at a closed-door meeting that it would process IPO applications already in the pipeline but wouldn’t take up new submissions for now, the people said. Officials also asked shareholders of listed companies to hold off from large-scale share sales until market conditions improve, the people said.

 

The guidance comes after a rough patch for the Chinese stock market. The economy is struggling, with car sales down 22% over the first nine months of this year, and investors are concerned that one of the few bright spots, the artificial intelligence boom, may be slowing down. The Shanghai Stock Exchange Composite Index fell 0.8% on Tuesday and has dropped more than 9% over the past two months.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

U.K. government bonds have been relatively calm following last month’s budget, but this could be short-lived, Economist Intelligence Unit’s Cailin Birch says in a note. The U.K. still faces fiscal challenges as the government didn’t address the difficult choices needed to meet fiscal rules, but rather pushed them into the future, the head of markets and insights says. “Meeting these [fiscal] targets would require significant spending restraint in 2028-29, a difficult sell directly before an election.” Ten-year gilt yields fell to a six-week low of 5.183% on Monday, before rising to last trade at 5.265%, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

 

Saudi Arabia’s quarterly budget deficit more than doubled in the third quarter to 84 billion riyals, according to data published by financial news portal Argaam. This marks an increase of 145% from the second quarter as the war in Iran and Houthi escalations continue to strain the kingdom’s public finances. Overall revenues for the first nine months of the year totaled 859 billion riyals, while spending was just over 1.1 trillion riyals, resulting in a deficit of 244 billion riyals. Oil revenues still comprised over half of that total, though non-oil revenues grew 8% from the same period last year. (joseph.wilkins@wsj.com)
